newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mafia runs nearly half Russian economy - US study.
newsitem.headline: Mafia runs nearly half Russian economy - US study.

text.p: Nearly half the Russian economy is controlled by organised criminals and billions of dollars are haemorrhaging out of Russia as a result, a U.S. study said.

"In Russia, organised crime groups are dominating both legitimate and illegitimate economic sectors simultaneously," said the study in the latest issue of the World Bank newsletter Transition, distributed in Moscow on Wednesday.

New criminal owners of enterprises are not interested in making their companies work but are draining their resources and transferring the proceeds abroad, exacerbating both capital flight and non-payment of wages, said the study, by Louise Shelley, a law professor at American University in Washington.

President Boris Yeltsin, in a keynote speech this month declaring a new war on crime and corruption, said mafia "godfathers" had hijacked the free market he created. He named a new reform-minded government this week but it faces an uphill task in rooting out deeply entrenched criminal interests.

Shelley, whose article is based on her forthcoming book "Stealing the Russian State", said organised crime, known in Russia as the mafia after Italy's bandit gangs, had seized control of more than 40 percent of the total Russian economy by taking advantage of the government's privatisation programme.
The mafia has an even greater share in sectors such as consumer markets, real estate and banking, she said.

"Russian organised crime groups secured a massive transfer of state property because the privatisation occurred rapidly, on a huge scale, without legal safeguards and without transparency," the study said.
Russia has transferred about 70 percent of enterprises to private hands since 1992.
"These groups used force, if necessary, but relied mainly on their large financial assets and their close ties to the former Communist Party elite, the military and the banking sector."

The strength of the mafia has contributed to a blurring in the eyes of ordinary Russians between crime and business. More than 70 years of Soviet propaganda denouncing private businessmen as crooks have also left their mark on attitudes.

In the Soviet period all private enterprise was illegal and could be severely punished, even by death. As a result many new entrepreneurs had semi-criminal origins and the breakdown of law and order allowed the mafia to run protection rackets.
Widespread corruption and bribe-taking among officials means many businessmen today must still resort to criminal methods.
As in other countries, mafia gangs launder their money by pouring it into legitimate businesses. But they have also infiltrated lucrative industries such as metals and banking.
The streets of Moscow are still relatively safe from Western-style crimes such as mugging. But gangland shootings and car-bombings of businessmen and bankers are relatively common.
Crime has an immediate impact on the economy.

"Organised crime...discourages foreign investment, deprives the country of its tax base, dominates the banking sector and financial markets, and exacerbates the already widespread problem of corruption," the study said.
But the most damaging aspect of Russian organised crime is its contribution to large-scale capital flight, it said.
Colombian drug traffickers repatriate most of their profits and the Italian mafia invested much of its profits domestically.
But Russian organised crime groups prefer to deposit most of their proceeds abroad, especially in off-shore havens, it said.
Conservative estimates of capital flight since 1991 are more than $50 billion, and one specialist at a recent Interior Ministry conference reported a figure of $150 billion, it said.

Organised crime also damages Russia's tax base. Apart from not paying taxes, organised crime groups usurp the state's tax collection role -- demanding protection money that eats heavily into small firms' profits -- depriving it of needed resources.
Suggesting ways to tackle the issue, the study said the problem must be seen as more than just money-laundering.

Donor nations and institutions must help set up regulation and enforcement mechanisms for effective governing of financial institutions and markets. Aid programmes must identify areas which have managed to avoid massive criminalisation.
"Building integrity in the banking sector and in financial markets must be a key objective of any assistance programme to combat Russian organised crime," it said.
